title: Urdu and Hindi, and your first letter
goal: Understand how Urdu relates to Hindi, write short messages and letters, and learn the visiting etiquette that makes you sound like an insider.
bekal: writing short messages and letters in Urdu
understanding why Urdu and Hindi are called one language in two scripts
using twenty expressions that open and close conversations

notes: **The form لکھیے گا isn't the future but a very gentle request.** It's used with guests, elders, and anyone you respect — and often for requests that aren't urgent at all. For example کھائیے گا · رکھیے گا · بتائیے گا. When you use it, your politeness instantly sounds mature.

**The phrase اپنا خیال رکھیے گا is the warmest way to say goodbye.** Literally "keep care of your own self" = "take care". Notice اپنا — the owner is the same as the subject, so it isn't آپ کا. The rule from unit 17 shows up again.

**The word ہی means "just, only, that very".** غلطیوں سے ہی زبان آتی ہے = "language comes precisely from mistakes". It attaches after the word you want to stress, and English has no one-word equivalent. Related: بھی (also), تو (indeed), صرف (only).
**The word کبھی means "ever, sometimes".** کبھی نہیں = "never". کبھی کبھی = "sometimes". کبھی نہ کبھی = "someday, sooner or later". Notice that نہیں comes after it, not before.

**The word افسوس expresses regret and sympathy.** ہمیں افسوس ہے = "we're sad". For news of a death, the sentence used is مجھے بہت افسوس ہوا ("I'm so sorry for your loss") — usually followed by إنا لله وإنا إليه راجعون.

**The word وجہ means "reason", and وجہ سے means "because of".** آپ کی وجہ سے = "because of you". Related words to keep apart: کیوں کہ ("because", opening a clause), اس لیے ("so, that's why", stating a result).

grammars.title: Urdu and Hindi: one language, two scripts, two formal vocabularies
body: This question always comes up, and the answer is more interesting than the usual one. In everyday spoken form, Urdu and Hindi **are the same language** — identical grammar, the same verbs, the same pronouns, the same word order. An Urdu speaker from Lahore and a Hindi speaker from Delhi can talk for hours without any trouble.

Two things set them apart, and both sit on the top layer: **the script** — Urdu uses Arabic letters in the Nastaliq style, Hindi uses Devanagari — and **the formal vocabulary**, which Urdu takes from Persian and Arabic, while Hindi takes it from Sanskrit.
after: Look at the last two rows: the most common words — water, home, eat, go, mother, hand — are **identical** in both languages, because both inherited them from ancient India. The differences only show up in formal words, literature, and the news.

What this means for you: once you finish this module, you can already **understand most Bollywood movies** and talk with Hindi speakers. All you can't do yet is **read Devanagari** — and that's a separate two-week project if you want it.

grammars.title: Writing messages and letters
body: Urdu messages on WhatsApp are much shorter and more casual than letters, but both have standard openings and closings. Know four opening lines and three closing lines, and you can write anything in between.

after: ⚠️ Written Urdu is usually **more formal** than spoken Urdu, even in short messages. A word you'd say as اچھا in conversation becomes بہتر in a letter. Sentences you cut short in conversation, you finish in a letter. When in doubt, write longer and more completely — in Urdu, that's never wrong.

blocks.title: Visiting etiquette you won't find in any book
items: **You'll be offered food, and the first refusal doesn't count.** Pakistani hosts offer three times, and accepting on the second offer is the polite middle ground. Only refusing three times in a row counts as a real no — and it's a little disappointing.

**Don't praise one particular object too specifically.** If you say "what a beautiful watch", there's a real chance the watch will be given to you, and refusing it gets complicated. Praise the atmosphere, the food, the house in general.

**A small gift is always right**: مٹھائی (sweets), fruit, or something from your own country. Hand it over with یہ آپ کے لیے ہے، بہت معمولی سی چیز ہے ("this is for you, it's just a little something") — playing down your own gift is part of the etiquette.

**Goodbyes take a long time, and that's normal.** A farewell conversation that goes on for fifteen minutes at the door isn't a sign you're being unclear — it's a sign the visit went well. The sentence that wraps it up: اچھا، اجازت دیجیے ("well then, allow me to take my leave").
